entry.title: three houses, one front door
entry.summary: Day eight of a hundred: a website concept for The Lights, three houses in Málaga's old town under one name, a social hostel, hotel-style suites and a hundred-year-old house with a garden.
entry.content:
On 25 November I posted the eighth note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in Estepona. That one is here. Day four was a private property practice in Málaga. That one is here. Day five was a tasting-menu restaurant in Motril. That one is here. Day six was a rotisserie chicken house in Estepona. That one is here. Day seven was a family-run hotel in Kavos, Corfu. That one is here.

Today is back on the Costa del Sol, in Málaga itself. The Lights is three places to stay in the old town under one name. The Lights Hostel is a boutique hostel in a historic Andalusian building. The Lights Suites are hotel-style private rooms in the same building, some with balconies over the Mercado Central. The Lights Garden is a traditional Andalusian house more than a hundred years old, a few streets away, with its own garden. Their current website is at thelights.es.

The concept is here: The Lights Málaga, day eight.

three houses, three guests

The difficulty here is not the design. It is the brief hiding inside the business.

A hostel, a set of suites and a quiet old house are three different products for three different people. The hostel is for solo travellers and groups of friends who want a terrace, a shared dinner and someone to go to the beach with. The suites are for couples and families who want a private room and a balcony, at a better price than a hotel. The garden house is for people who want peace after a long day in the sun, and often for longer stays.

Put all three on one website and the usual result is a page that talks to nobody. The hostel guest reads about quiet gardens. The family reads about bunk beds and parties. And nobody can find the booking button, because there are three of them in three different places.

So the challenge was to bring them together under one identity, the same name, the same team and the same free extras, while letting each house keep its own character. And to make three things impossible to miss on every screen: where it is, what kind of room you are getting, and how to book it directly.

Day eight: three houses in the heart of Málaga’s old town, a short stroll from the sea.

a summer front page

Málaga sells summer. Most people who book a bed in the old town are coming for the sun, the sea and long evenings out, so the first screen says exactly that.

The background is a photograph of the port at Muelle Uno: palm trees, the lighthouse, tall ships and the water. On top, in a large serif in deep sea blue, the line your summer in Málaga starts here, with the last two words in terracotta italics. A small drawn sun turns slowly in the corner. Above the headline, three words in small capitals: hostel, suites, garden. That is the whole business in three words, before anyone has scrolled.

Under the headline, one sentence: three charming houses in the heart of the old town, next to the Mercado Central and a short stroll from the sea. Then two buttons, check availability and discover our houses.

The logo is the one The Lights already uses, a round blue badge with a lamp, sitting in the middle of the header. I did not redraw it. The header around it has the six sections the business already uses, Home, Accommodations, Facilities, Offers, Blog and Contact Us, and a terracotta Book now button on the right.

The light theme: cream pages, sea-blue type and terracotta buttons, with the port and the three houses up front.

the booking bar comes first

Directly under the hero, overlapping the bottom of the photograph, there is a booking bar. Where, arrival, departure, guests, search. It is the first thing you can actually use on the page.

Where is a choice of the three houses. The dates already hold sensible defaults, tomorrow and three nights later, so a visitor only has to change what is different. Guests go from one to six, and then seven or more, a group. On a phone the bar stacks into a neat form, one field above the other, with a large search button at the bottom.

Under the bar, four short promises, each with a tick: best price guaranteed, free breakfast, free sangría, free Wi-Fi. These are the four things a guest compares between booking sites, and here they are written before the guest has to go looking for them.

To be clear about what the concept does at that point: the search button sends the dates, the house and the number of guests to The Lights’ current website. Each house has its own booking system, and in a real build the button would open the right one, with the dates already filled in. That connection is the first job on the list if the concept goes further.

Pick a house, then a date. The four promises sit under the search bar on every visit.

three houses, one Málaga

The heart of the page is a section called three houses, one Málaga. Its first line says what the three have in common: the same friendly team and the same free extras. Choose the style that suits your summer.

Then three cards, side by side on a computer and one after another on a phone. Each has a photograph in an arched frame, a nod to the doorways and windows of old Andalusian houses, a colour of its own and a line saying who it is for.

The Lights Hostel is blue, for solo travellers and friends: a boutique hostel in an emblematic historic Andalusian building, social, central and easy to love, with a terrace made for meeting people. Terrace, themed dinners, luggage storage.

The Lights Suites are terracotta, for couples and families: hotel-level comfort at hostel prices, with superior rooms whose balconies look straight over the Mercado Central. Private rooms, market-view balconies, breakfast.

The Lights Garden is olive green, for slow, peaceful stays: a traditional Andalusian house more than a hundred years old in the historic centre, a green, quiet hideaway after a long day of sun. A hundred-year-old house, the garden, long stays.

Each card ends with its own button, book the hostel, book the suites, book the garden, which takes you back up to the booking bar with that house already chosen. And under each button, the address, because two of the houses share one and the garden has another. A guest who books the garden should never turn up at the hostel.

Those three colours, blue, terracotta and olive, run through the whole page. Once you have seen them in the cards, you know which house a button or a line of text is about without reading the label.

A hostel for friends, suites for couples and families, and a hundred-year-old Andalusian house with a garden.

the little things are on us

Hostels in Málaga compete on price, and price on a booking site always looks similar. What differs is what is included. The Lights includes a lot, and their current site mentions it only in passing.

So there is a section for it, called the little things are on us, with a plain line underneath: no extra charges for the good stuff. Eight small cards follow. Free sangría, a cold glass of welcome every stay. Free breakfast, to start your beach day properly. Free themed dinners, shared tables and new friends. Fast Wi-Fi, free everywhere in the house. A sunny terrace, sun by day and sangría by night. Luggage storage, for the early flight or the late check-in. Maps and tips from the team. And groups welcome, with tailored offers for big groups. The first three wear a small terracotta free tag, because those are the ones nobody expects.

There is also a round yellow sticker on the welcome section that reads free sangría, every guest, every stay, turning slowly like a badge on a suitcase. It is the friendliest line on the page, so it gets to move.

sun, sea and the city

Before the extras, there is a full-width photograph of the sign at La Malagueta, the city beach, and a short invitation: leave the car at home. From the door, Málaga’s best summer days are all within walking distance.

Beside it, the walking times, written the way you would plan a day. Muelle Uno and the port, about twelve minutes. La Malagueta beach, about twenty. The beaches at Pedregalejo and El Palo, a short bus ride. Sunset at the Gibralfaro, about twenty-five minutes on foot. These are the questions people ask at reception on their first morning, answered before they arrive.

Walking times to the port, the beach and the Gibralfaro, and the free sangría, breakfast and dinners that come with every stay.

the best address in town

The single strongest argument for The Lights is where it is, so the location is not tucked away in the footer. It has a section of its own, called the best address in town.

On one side, a photograph of the cathedral, which the people of Málaga call La Manquita, the one-armed lady, because its second tower was never finished. On the other, a numbered list of walking times from the door on Calle Torregorda, each in a round badge. One minute to the Mercado Central de Atarazanas, for fresh fish, fruit and tapas bars. Five minutes to Calle Larios, the main shopping street. Eight minutes to the cathedral and the old town squares. Ten minutes to the Picasso Museum and the Alcazaba. Twenty minutes to La Malagueta beach. A small note at the bottom says these are approximate, which they are.

The numbers do the selling. One minute to the market says more about the location than any adjective could.

A walking-time guide to the market, Calle Larios and the beach, plus both addresses, phones and emails.

book direct and save

Every booking a hostel takes through a large platform costs it a commission. The Lights already promises its best price on its own website, and says so in small letters in its header. The concept says it in large ones.

There is a section called always the best price here, with one honest line: skip the booking platforms; when you book on our own website you always get our lowest rate, plus a few extras only we can offer. Then four reasons. Best price guaranteed. A followers’ discount, with an exclusive code for people who follow them on social media. Group offers, a tailored price for a crowd. And special rates for long stays in Málaga. One button, check availability, takes you back to the booking bar.

The same promise runs along the top bar of every screen, book on our website, best price guaranteed, in gold. And once you have scrolled past the booking bar on a phone, a slim bar appears at the bottom of the screen with the name, the line best price, booked direct, and a book now button. It stays there until you leave.

we’ll leave a light on for you

The contact section takes its title from the name of the business: we’ll leave a light on for you. It is the kind of line a small hotel would write on a handwritten note.

Underneath are two cards, one per address, because The Lights is in two places. Hostel and suites at Calle Torregorda 3, with its phone number, its email, a button for directions and one for WhatsApp. The Garden at Calle Molinillo del Aceite 5, with its own phone, its own email and its own directions. Each card is edged with its house’s colour, blue for the hostel and suites, green for the garden, so the two never get mixed up.

a menu that slides down

On a phone, the header keeps three things: the menu button, the logo in the middle and book now. Above it, a thin bar with the phone number and the light and dark switch.

Tap the menu and it slides down to fill the screen, and the three lines of the button turn into a cross. The six sections appear in large serif type, with a full-width book now button under them and the address and phone number at the bottom, where a thumb can reach them. It works the same in both themes.

Big type, a booking button, the address and the phone number.

the same welcome after sunset

Like the hotel in Corfu yesterday, The Lights has a light theme and a dark one. A small switch with a sun and a moon sits next to book now on a computer and in the top bar on a phone.

The light theme is a Málaga morning: cream and sand pages, deep sea-blue type, terracotta buttons and touches of sun yellow. The dark theme is the same city after sunset: deep navy pages, cream type, the same terracotta and the yellow turning gold. Both were designed section by section, not inverted. The site remembers the choice for the next visit, and if a visitor has never touched the switch, it follows whatever their phone or computer is already set to.

A sun-and-moon switch turns the cream pages to deep navy, and the site remembers the choice.

One toggle changes the light: both themes, side by side.

the details

The type is DM Serif Display for the headlines, set large, with italics in terracotta for the warmer words: starts here, one Málaga, light on. Jost, a clean geometric sans, for everything you read, in spaced capitals for the small labels and buttons.

The colours are the city’s: the deep blue of the sea and of The Lights’ own logo, terracotta from the rooftops, sand and cream from the old town walls, sun yellow, and olive green for the garden. A thin dashed line in blue and yellow, like the edge of a beach towel, separates some of the sections.

Things fade in gently as you scroll, the hero photo drifts very slowly, and the sun and the sangría sticker turn. All of it stops for visitors who have asked their phone or computer to reduce motion, and the page works exactly the same without it. The fonts are served from my own site rather than from Google, so loading the page does not hand a visitor’s address to anyone else.

what the concept is, and what comes next

The facts on the page, the three houses, their addresses, phone numbers and emails, the free extras, the offers and the best-price promise, come from The Lights’ current website. Their logo and the sections of their menu are kept as they are. The walking times are approximate, and the page says so.

What is new is the structure: one identity that holds three different houses, a booking bar that comes before everything else, a colour for each house, the extras turned into a reason to book direct, and a location section that lets the numbers speak.

I have no figures on bookings, and I will not make any up. Turning the concept into a working site would take the practical steps: connecting each house to its own booking system so the dates carry across, a Spanish version alongside the English, the blog and the offers pages, and the team’s own photographs everywhere they have them.

if you run more than one place

You may not run a hostel. Plenty of businesses on this coast have more than one place under one name, though: a restaurant group with a beach bar and a town restaurant, a holiday rental company with apartments in three villages, a gym with two locations, a language school with a summer campus.

What helps is the same as here. Say what they have in common first, then let each place keep its own character. Give each one a colour and stick to it. Put every address next to the thing it belongs to, never only in the footer. Make the location a reason to choose you, with real distances rather than adjectives. And put the booking button where people look first, not where there was space left.

I am a web designer based in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I design and build websites for businesses in Spain and beyond. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The concept is here, and The Lights’ current site is here, so you can compare the two. Eight down, ninety-two to go.

entry.title: the same pool after dark
entry.summary: Day seven of a hundred: a website concept for Morfeas Hotel, a family-run hotel in Kavos, Corfu, that changes with the time of day, from a pool in the sun to the same pool under the moon.
entry.content:
On 23 November I posted the seventh note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in Estepona. That one is here. Day four was a private property practice in Málaga. That one is here. Day five was a tasting-menu restaurant in Motril. That one is here. Day six was a rotisserie chicken house in Estepona. That one is here.

Today is the first business of the run outside Spain. Morfeas Hotel is a family-run hotel with rooms and apartments in Kavos, at the southern tip of Corfu. It is a minute from the Ionian Sea and a few minutes’ walk from the main street of Kavos, which is famous for one thing: going out. The hotel is named after Morpheus, the Greek god of dreams. Its own website is at morfeashotel.com.

The concept is here: Morfeas Hotel, day seven.

This is an independent redesign concept. It is not an official collaboration with Morfeas Hotel, nobody there asked me for it, and nothing on the page means they have approved it. Like the six before it, it lives on my own address for now.

one hotel, two holidays

Most hotel websites describe one holiday. A pool, a room, a breakfast, a sunset. That works for a quiet hotel. It does not work for a hotel in Kavos.

Guests at Morfeas have two holidays in the same week, sometimes in the same day. By day it is the pool: loungers, cold drinks, the resident DJ. By night it is dinner from the hotel kitchen, then the party, either at the hotel or on the strip around the corner. The same people, the same pool, two different moods. The hotel already puts this in one of its lines: dream by day, dance by night.

So instead of choosing one of the two, the concept shows both, and lets the visitor decide which one they are looking at.

Day seven: one hotel, one pool, two moods.

slide from day to night

The top of the page is a drawing rather than a photograph: the white hotel building with its blue shutters, a beach umbrella, two loungers, the sea behind and a pool in the foreground. The word Morfeas sits across it in a large serif, as big as the screen allows.

The drawing exists twice, once by day and once by night, laid exactly on top of each other. A small handle with a sun on one side and a moon on the other sits in the middle. Drag it, and the line between the two drawings moves with your finger. On the left, a pale blue sky and the line dream by day. On the right, a navy sky, stars, a crescent moon, a palm tree in silhouette, a string of party lights over the water and a beam of light rising from the pool. The line there reads dance by night. Drag the handle all the way and the whole hotel goes from noon to midnight.

When the page opens, the handle is not in the middle. It leans towards whatever time it is in Kavos. A visitor arriving in the afternoon sees mostly day. Someone looking at eleven at night, Corfu time, sees mostly night. A small clock in the header shows the time in Kavos with a sun or a moon beside it, which is a small thing but useful for anyone planning a holiday from another time zone.

I drew the scene instead of using photographs for two reasons. A drawing can change from day to night without a second photo shoot. And at a small size on a phone, a simple drawing reads faster than a busy photograph of a pool full of people.

Drag the handle and the poolside turns from noon to midnight. When the page opens, it leans towards the time in Kavos.

a light theme and a dark one

The hero is not the only thing that changes. The whole site has a light theme and a dark one.

The light theme is a pool day: white pages, the deep Aegean blue of Greek shutters and doors, and touches of lemon yellow. The dark theme is the same site after sunset: deep navy pages, light blue for links and buttons, the same lemon yellow. Neither is an afterthought. I designed both, section by section, so that the dark version is not just the light one with the colours inverted.

A button with a moon or a sun in the header switches between them. The site remembers the choice for the next visit. If a visitor has never pressed it, the site follows whatever their phone or computer is already set to. Switching the theme also moves the hero handle, so the drawing at the top agrees with the rest of the page.

The light theme: white pages, Aegean blue and lemon yellow, with the family’s own note near the top.

The dark theme. One tap on the moon and the whole site turns navy, and it stays that way next time.

a note from the family

Under the hero, the first thing to read is not a list of services. It is a short note from the family, signed in handwriting: Morfeas is a family-run hotel at the southern tip of Corfu, a minute from the sea and a few minutes’ walk from the main street. By day, the pool. By night, dinner from their own kitchen and then the party. Stay a week and you leave feeling like part of the family.

Beside it, three numbers in large type: 55 rooms and apartments, one minute to the sea, 30 kilometres from the airport. They answer the three questions people ask about any island hotel before they ask anything else: how big is it, how far is the sea, how far is the airport.

your key to Kavos

The accommodation section is called your key to Kavos, and each type of stay has a key-tag of its own, the old-fashioned kind that hangs from a room key at reception. A blue one for the hotel rooms. A yellow one for the apartments. They swing gently when they come into view.

The rooms are double or twin, each with its own balcony, air conditioning, a television, a safe, a hair dryer and a shower room. The apartments have more space, for friends and families travelling together, with cots on request and free parking. Each type has a button to check dates, which opens the booking drawer with that type already selected.

a menu that fills the screen

On a phone, the header shrinks to three things: the logo, a Book button and the menu button. Tap the menu and it fills the whole screen with the six sections of the site in large italic serif letters, an online reservation button, and a Greek key border along the bottom, the pattern you see on plates and tiles all over the islands. It works the same in both themes.

Once you scroll past the top, a bar settles at the bottom of the screen with two things in it: check availability, and a button that calls reception. On a hotel website, booking should never be more than a tap away.

The menu fills the screen: big serif links, a booking button and a Greek key border, in light or dark.

pick a mood, get a day plan

This is the part I would most like a hotel to steal.

People do not choose a hotel in Kavos for its towels. They choose it for the kind of holiday they want. So the section asks: how do you holiday? There are four answers, as buttons: sun-seeker, night owl, foodie, and friends and family. Pick one, and the site sketches out a day at Morfeas for that kind of guest, hour by hour.

The sun-seeker’s day is all about the pool: breakfast at ten, then first pick of the loungers, the DJ at one, the hot tub and a cocktail at four, a walk down to the sea before dinner. The night owl’s day starts at noon on the balcony, with no alarm, warms up at the pool party at three, goes to Greek Night or a theme night at nine and reaches the strip at midnight. The foodie’s day is built around breakfast, the pool bar and dinner at the hotel restaurant. The friends and family day ends with everyone on the balcony, because every room and apartment has one.

Every line of those plans comes from things the hotel actually has. Nothing is invented to make the day sound better. The point is that a visitor sees themselves in it, and in four lines knows whether this is their kind of hotel. You can also move between the four moods with the arrow keys on a keyboard.

Four holiday moods. Each one sketches a different day at the hotel, hour by hour.

three nights to remember

The evening at Morfeas has three regular events: the pool party, Greek Night and theme nights. On most hotel websites they would be three lines in a list. Here they are three posters, the kind you would see taped up by the reception desk.

The pool party poster is lemon yellow with wavy lines like water. Greek Night is white with a blue Greek key border and Opa! written by hand across the top. Theme nights is navy with a big yellow moon. On a computer they lean against each other like posters on a wall. On a phone you swipe through them one by one, with small dots to show where you are. Above them, one honest line: ask at reception what’s on during your stay. Dates change every season, and a website that promises a date it cannot keep is worse than one that sends you to the desk.

Next comes the food, with the hotel restaurant, breakfast, the pool bar, dinner and the music lounge, and a link to the menus. Then the facilities: the outdoor pool, the resident DJ, the hot tub, two bars, the restaurant, air conditioning, free Wi-Fi, free parking and a reception that is open 24 hours.

Pool Party, Greek Night and Theme Nights as hand-made posters you can swipe through on a phone.

your stay, in one drawer

Every booking button on the page, whether in the header, under a room type or at the bottom, opens the same thing: a drawer that slides in from the side, called your stay. It asks for four things: check-in date, check-out date, a hotel room or an apartment, and how many guests, from one adult up to two adults and two children.

It counts the nights as you go and writes it back in one line: 7 nights, apartment, 3 adults. Then it hands you on to the hotel’s secure booking page. If a date is missing, it says so and puts the cursor in the right field, rather than letting you press the button and wonder why nothing happened.

At the bottom of the drawer there is one more line: prefer to talk? Call reception, with the number ready to tap. Plenty of people still book a family holiday by phone, and the drawer treats that as a perfectly good answer.

To be clear about what the concept does at that point: the drawer gathers the details and sends the visitor to the hotel’s current website. It does not pass the dates across in the concept. In a real build it would open the hotel’s booking system with the dates and room type already filled in.

Choose dates, room type and guests. It counts the nights, then hands you on. Every drawer ends with a number to call.

a postcard from Kavos

The contact section is a postcard. It is headed wish you were here. On the left half there is a hand-drawn map of the south of Corfu in blue and white, with a yellow pin and we’re here written beside it in handwriting. On the right, where you would write the message, there is a short note: the sea’s a minute away, the strip’s round the corner, come and stay. Under that, the distances: the Ionian Sea, one minute’s walk; the centre of Kavos and the strip, 0.2 km; Kavos beach, 1.2 km; the port at Lefkimmi, 5 km; Corfu airport, 30 km. In the corner there is a stamp, a Greek key tile with a little yellow sun, and a postmark.

Then the guest rating, as large as the hotel’s name at the top: 4.6 out of 5, the average from 1,340 guest reviews on easyJet holidays, as it appears on the hotel’s own site. A line from the family, a button to check availability and the phone number. A Greek key border closes the page.

A hand-drawn postcard with the distances that matter, and the guest rating front and centre.

the details

The type is DM Serif Display for the headlines, set large and tight, with italics for the warmer words. Jost, a clean geometric sans, for everything you read. Caveat, a handwriting face, for the family’s signature, Opa! and we’re here.

The colours stay close to the island: the Aegean blue of shutters and doors, a deep night navy, lemon yellow and plenty of white. The logo is the hotel’s own.

Headlines rise into place word by word as you scroll, sections fade in, the key-tags swing and the stars over the night pool twinkle. All of it switches off for visitors who have asked their phone or computer to reduce motion, and the page works exactly the same without it. The day-and-night handle can be moved with the keyboard as well as the mouse or a finger.

what the concept is, and what it is not

The facts on the page come from the hotel’s current website and public listings: the rooms and apartments, the facilities, the events, the address, the phone numbers, the distances and the guest rating. The family note and the day plans are my own writing, built only from those facts. If the family ever wanted it, they would replace my words with theirs.

What is new is the way it all fits together: one hotel shown in two moods, a page that knows what time it is in Kavos, a planner that speaks to the kind of guest rather than the kind of room, and a booking step that never makes you leave the page until you are ready.

I have no figures on bookings, and I will not make any up. If nobody at Morfeas wants this, the concept stays where it is as day seven. If they do, the rest is practical: their own words in place of mine, their photographs alongside the drawings, the booking drawer connected to their booking system, a Greek version, and the site moved onto morfeashotel.com.

if your business changes with the hour

You may not run a hotel in Kavos. A lot of businesses still have two faces, though: a beach bar that turns into a cocktail bar, a café that serves dinner, a restaurant with a quiet lunch and a loud Saturday night, a venue that hosts weddings by day and concerts by night. Their websites usually show only one of the two, and the other half of the customers have to guess.

What helps is the same as here. Show both moods, and let people choose. Use the time of day if it matters. Describe the experience in the order a guest lives it, not in the order of your price list. Keep the booking button within reach on every screen. And always leave a phone number for the people who would rather talk.

I am a web designer based in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I design and build websites for businesses in Spain and beyond. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The concept is here, and Morfeas Hotel’s current site is here, so you can compare the two. Seven down, ninety-three to go.

entry.title: from the counter to the ticket
entry.summary: Day six of a hundred: a website concept for El Dorado, a rotisserie chicken house in Estepona, where you order the way you would at the counter and watch your ticket print as you go.
entry.content:
On 22 November I posted the sixth note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in Estepona. That one is here. Day four was a private property practice in Málaga. That one is here. Day five was a tasting-menu restaurant in Motril. That one is here.

Today is the most everyday business of the six, and maybe the one whose website gets used most often. El Dorado is a rotisserie chicken house on Avenida Puerta del Mar in Estepona, my own town. Roast chicken, chips, home-made croquettes, burgers, sandwiches, Argentine empanadas, sauces, drinks. You can order for delivery or for pick-up, every day, at lunch and in the evening. It already has a website and an online shop, at pollosasadosadomicilioestepona.es.

A roast chicken website has two jobs. It should make you hungry, and it should make ordering easy. Most takeaway sites manage one of the two. The concept is here: El Dorado, day six.

the counter, not the catalogue

Think about how you order at the counter of a chicken shop. You do not start by browsing. The person behind the counter asks two questions first: is it to take away or to eat at home, and for when? Only then do you say what you want. A whole chicken, a large chips, some croquettes, a bottle of cola. They write it on a ticket, read it back to you, tell you the total.

Most online ordering does this backwards. It shows you a shop full of products, lets you fill a basket, and only at the very end, at the checkout, asks whether you want delivery and at what time. That is where people find out the slot they wanted is gone, or that delivery does not reach their street, and they give up.

So the concept copies the counter. The first thing on the page, under the headline, is a small panel with two questions. 01: how do you want it, a domicilio or para recoger, delivered or for pick-up. 02: for when, lo antes posible, as soon as possible, or a set time from a row of buttons, 13:30, 14:30, 20:00, 21:00, or another time. Then one dark button: 03, elegir mi pedido, choose my order. It takes you down to the menu.

You tell the shop how you want it before you even see the menu. That is how the person at the counter would do it, and it means the rest of the page already knows what you are planning.

The opening: the headline, the chicken, and the two questions the counter would ask first.

How, when, then the menu. Like ordering at the counter.

a chicken on the page

The headline is the plainest sentence I could write: pollo asado al fuego, directo a tu puerta. Roast chicken from the fire, straight to your door. It is set very large in a heavy, slightly squashed sans, in cream and gold, with al fuego in a thin italic serif in between. It reads like the sign on a shopfront.

Next to it is the thing people actually come for: a roast chicken, golden and glistening, herbs on the skin. I cut it out of its photograph so it sits directly on the dark brown page, without a box around it. A slow ring of text turns around it, un sabor único, pollos asados, Estepona, which is El Dorado’s own line. There is a warm glow behind it, a few embers rising, and on a computer it tilts very slightly towards your cursor.

I know how that sounds on paper. On the screen it is quiet. The point is to make the first thing you see the food, at a size where you can almost smell it.

Cut out from its backdrop, so it sits right on the page. A warm glow, a few embers, and a ring of text turning slowly.

the real menu, every price

The second section is called haz tu comanda, make your order. A comanda is the Spanish word for the order ticket the kitchen works from, and the whole idea of this concept rests on it.

On the left are the nine categories from El Dorado’s own menu, each with the number of dishes in it: chicken and fried sides, burgers, sandwiches, baguettes, home-made croquettes, empanadas, things to share, sauces and drinks. In the middle are the dishes of the chosen category, numbered like a menu board, each with a short description and its price. On the right is the ticket.

I did not simplify the menu to make the design easier. A real chicken shop has sizes, and sizes are where online ordering usually goes wrong. Half a chicken is 7 euros and a whole one 12. Chips are 2.50 small and 4 large. Croquettes come in fives and tens. A bottle of cola is a litre or two. So every size has its own price and its own plus button. You do not choose a size from a menu and then press add. You press the plus next to the size you want. The total is always right, because there is no step in between where it can go wrong.

The wings list their nine sauces, from garlic and parmesan to Carolina Reaper. The burgers say what they are made of, 100% beef. And under the categories there is a small link to the full menu as a PDF, the one El Dorado already publishes, for anyone who prefers to read it all at once.

All nine categories from El Dorado’s own menu. Each size has its own price and its own plus button, so the total is always right.

the ticket prints as you order

This is the part I enjoyed most. As you add things, they appear on a ticket on the right of the screen, drawn like the paper slips that come out of a kitchen printer: cream paper, a typewriter typeface, a zigzag torn edge at the bottom.

At the top it says comanda number 981, or whatever number it gives you, with the time. Then asador de pollos El Dorado, and the address. Then the two answers you gave at the start: a domicilio, lo antes posible. Then each line as you add it: 1 roast chicken, whole, 12 euros. 1 chips, large, 4 euros. 1 ham croquettes, 10, 7 euros. 1 bottle of cola, 2 litres, 2.50. A count of items, and the total, 25.50 euros.

Every time you add something, a small message slides in at the bottom of the screen to confirm it: added, bottle of cola, 2 litres, with a link to see the ticket. If you change your mind, the plus turns into a minus and a number.

Under the total there is a line about delivery terms, a field for the delivery address, and a button: finalizar pedido online, finish the order online. Below it, in small letters, the alternative: o pídelo por teléfono, or order by phone, 952 63 33 18.

To be clear about what the concept does at that point: the button takes you to El Dorado’s existing online shop to complete the order there. The items on the ticket are not passed across in the concept. In a real build, the ticket is exactly what the kitchen would receive, either into the shop they already use or straight to a printer behind the counter. The design is the part that matters for the customer: you can see your order the whole time, in the same form the kitchen will.

Each dish prints onto a paper-style ticket, with a zigzag edge, an order number, the time and a running total.

always shows if it is open

Nothing is more annoying than ordering from a takeaway that turns out to be closed. El Dorado opens every day from 10:30 to 16:00 and from 19:00 to 22:00, and the concept says so everywhere it matters.

A gold bar runs across the very top of the page. When the shop is open it reads abierto ahora, pedidos hasta las 16:00, open now, orders until 16:00, or until 22:00 in the evening. When it is closed, it says when it opens again, at 10:30 or at 19:00, and adds programa tu pedido, schedule your order. Nobody is turned away. They are told when to come back, and that they can order ahead.

Further down, the hours section has a 24-hour clock face. The two opening periods are drawn as arcs around the edge, lunch in gold and evening in caramel, and the hand shows the real time in Estepona. At 13:42 it sits inside the lunch arc and the centre says abierto ahora. Next to it: abiertos todos los días, open every day, the two time slots, the address on Avenida Puerta del Mar, a button for directions and the phone number.

The clock reads the time in Estepona, not on your phone, so it is right even for someone ordering for their parents from London.

The gold top bar and the 24-hour clock read the real time in Estepona. The hand moves across the lunch and evening arcs.

made for one thumb

Most orders from a place like this happen on a phone, with one hand, often while doing something else. So I designed the phone version first and the large screen after.

At the bottom of the screen there is a bar that never moves: mi comanda, with the number of items, and llamar, call. Tap the first and you jump to your ticket. Tap the second and your phone dials the shop. Whatever you are looking at, ordering or calling is one tap away.

On a phone, the categories are not a row you have to scroll sideways, which is easy to miss. They are a grid of large buttons, two per row, so all nine are visible at once and each one is big enough for a thumb. The confirmation message appears just above the bottom bar, where your eyes already are.

The menu opens over the whole screen, with the gold opening-status bar at the top, the five sections of the site, a large button to call the shop on 952 63 33 18, and the chicken again at the bottom.

A sticky bar with the ticket and a call button. Categories as big tap targets, with no sideways scrolling.

their brand, as it is

Every concept in this run so far has had a new look. This one does not, and on purpose.

El Dorado already has a brand that people in Estepona know: a logo with a chicken in front of flames and a ribbon reading asador de pollos El Dorado. It is not a minimalist logo, and it does not need to be. It is the sign over the shop. So I kept it, cleaned up and enlarged to stay sharp on modern screens, and built everything else around it.

The colours come from the logo as well. Espresso, #24190F, for the background. Brown, #876445. Caramel, #CA965C. Gold, #EEC373, for buttons and the top bar. Cream, #F4DFBA, for the ticket and the light sections. On a dark page they look like the inside of a rotisserie, which is the point.

The type is new. Bricolage Grotesque, heavy and tightly spaced, for the big headlines, so they read like a shop sign. Instrument Serif in italic for the warmer words. Space Mono, a typewriter face, for the ticket and the small labels. Inter for everything you need to read quickly.

There is also a section about the house: un sabor único, sin atajos, a unique flavour, no shortcuts. They roast every day and make at home what can be made at home: chicken, ham and spinach croquettes, and burgers with 100% beef. Next to it, three real customer reviews, held on with strips of paper tape like notes on a fridge. One customer calls El Dorado the best rotisserie on the whole Costa del Sol. Another praises one of the few places where you order for a set time and they keep it.

El Dorado’s own logo, three real customer reviews, and the five-colour palette taken from the brand.

motion with restraint

A few small things move on this page, and each one has a job. The lines of the headline slide up one by one as the page loads. Sections fade in as you scroll to them. The rotisserie photo in the house section drifts slightly. A thin gold line along the top of the header shows how far down the page you are.

Between the sections there is a short story in three words, the way a shop might paint it on the wall. Pides. Asamos. Disfrutas. You order, online or by phone. We roast, every day, lunch and evening, here in Estepona. You enjoy, ready at the agreed time, still hot. At the very bottom of the page, El Dorado is written very large in the footer, with a slow sheen across it.

All of the motion switches off for visitors who have asked their phone or computer to reduce motion. The page works exactly the same without it.

Bold type, italic serif, reviews taped on like notes, and motion that switches off when asked.

what the concept is, and what comes next

El Dorado’s logo, colours, menu, prices, hours, address, phone number and customer reviews on the page are their own. I have not changed any of them. What is new is the order of things, the ticket, the clock and the way the page behaves on a phone.

Two things would need to happen to turn the concept into a working shop. First, the ticket has to reach the kitchen: either into the online shop El Dorado already runs, or as a printed ticket behind the counter. Second, the time slots should come from the kitchen itself, so that a busy Sunday lunch can close a slot before it fills up. Neither is complicated. Both are worth doing properly.

I have no figures for orders or takings, and I will not make any up.

if people order from you on their phone

You may not sell roast chicken. A lot of small businesses on this coast take orders, though: a bakery that does cakes to order, a pizzeria, a florist, a laundry, a butcher who prepares barbecue packs for the weekend. Their customers usually order from a phone, in a hurry, and the website usually asks them to think like a shop assistant.

What helps is the same as here. Ask how and when first. Show every option with its own price. Let people see their order the whole time, in the form you will receive it. Say clearly whether you are open, and if not, when. And keep the phone number one tap away, because some people will always prefer to call.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The concept is here, and El Dorado’s current site is here, so you can compare the two. Six down, ninety-four to go.

entry.title: as careful as the kitchen
entry.summary: Day five of a hundred: a website concept for Espacio IME, Iván Mateo's tasting-menu restaurant in Motril, built to sit beside its guide listings without looking out of place.
entry.content:
On 21 November I posted the fifth note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in my own town, Estepona. That one is here. Day four was a private property practice in Málaga. That one is here. Today is a restaurant again, but a very different one.

Espacio IME is a small tasting-menu restaurant in Motril, on the Costa Tropical, the stretch of the Granada coast where mangoes, avocados and custard apples grow a few minutes from the sea. The chef is Iván Mateo. He came home to Motril after eleven years cooking in restaurants around Spain, and he has run IME since December 2021. His cooking is built on local produce: fish from the Motril market, the coast’s subtropical fruit, Granada wines.

The guides have noticed. Espacio IME is a recommended restaurant in the Repsol Guide for 2026. It is selected in the Michelin Guide. Macarfi, the guide that scores restaurants on food, setting and service, gives it a card of its own and singles out a rice with Motril shrimp as worth the trip by itself.

Some restaurants deserve websites as good as the food they serve. The concept is here: Espacio IME, day five. The restaurant’s own website is at espacioime.es, and its Instagram is @espacioime.

This is an independent design concept. It is not a collaboration with Espacio IME, nobody there asked me for it, and nothing on the page means they have approved it. Like the four before it, it lives on my own address for now.

a website that belongs next to the awards

Think about how people arrive at a restaurant like this. Hardly anyone finds a tasting menu in Motril by walking past. They read about it in a guide, see a plate on Instagram, hear about it from a friend who drove down from Granada. Then they look it up. The website is the second impression, and it comes straight after a guide has told them this place is worth a special trip.

If the website then looks like a template, with stock photos and a contact form in a corner, the visitor feels the gap. Not because a template is a crime, but because everything else about the place says care: the produce, the plating, the short wine list, the small room. The website is the only part of the experience the restaurant gives away for free, to everybody, before they have tasted anything.

So I set myself a simple brief. The site should show the same attention to detail as the kitchen. A clear order, the produce at the front, the menus with their prices, the wine, the gift, and a calm way to ask for a table. Nothing that shouts.

a journey through the flavours of the coast

The site opens in the dining room. A wide photograph of the room fills the screen, darkened so the text sits on it comfortably: wooden tables, mustard chairs, a vase of dried flowers.

The headline is set in a tall, narrow serif: un viaje por los sabores de la Costa Tropical, a journey through the flavours of the Costa Tropical. The last two words are in italic and in a soft gold. Above it is a small line, cocina de autor, Motril, Granada, which is how a guide would describe the place. Below it, one sentence: the intimate restaurant of Iván Mateo, where art and food live together, with market fish, subtropical fruit and the sea in every course.

Then two buttons: book a table, or discover the menus. At the bottom of the screen, a white plate rises into view, with a line of text running around its rim like the edge of a ceramic stamp: Costa Tropical, Motril, cocina de autor, Iván Mateo.

Just under the opening sits a quiet row with the three recognitions: the Michelin Guide 2026, the Repsol Guide 2026 and Macarfi. They are small and set in the same type as everything else, and the footer links to the restaurant’s pages in the Michelin and Repsol guides. Awards work best when they are easy to check and not shouted.

The opening on a large screen, and the experience section on two phones.

every plate starts with the land

The first section after the opening is about the cook, not the menu. Its heading reads: cada plato nace de la tierra, la estación y el amor por el oficio. Every plate starts with the land, the season and a love of the craft.

Next to it is one quotation from the kitchen, set large in italic with a thin gold line beside it: our cooking is not only technique, it is a way of life. Then a short paragraph. After eleven years cooking in restaurants across Spain, Iván Mateo came back to his home town. Here he works with fresh, local, seasonal produce from trusted suppliers nearby, with precision, order and the greatest respect for the ingredient.

Three figures close the section. 2021, open since December. 4, new menus every year. 11, years in kitchens across Spain. I prefer figures like these to adjectives. A guest can check every one of them, and together they say more about the place than “exceptional” ever could.

the produce, by name

A tasting menu is hard to describe in advance, because it changes. What does not change is where it comes from. So between the story and the menus there is a band of ingredients, with a small drawing for each one and a line underneath.

Quisquilla de Motril, the local shrimp, the jewel of the coast. Fish from the market, from the port of Motril. Mango, grown on the Costa Tropical. Avocado, subtropical and local. Chirimoya, the custard apple, Granada’s sweet fruit. And the wines of Granada, a short and personal list.

The same names run across the screen as a slow ticker further up, in gold italic, one after another. A visitor from Madrid or London may not know what a quisquilla is. After this page, they will want to try one.

two journeys, one coast

The menus come next, under the heading dos viajes, una misma costa: two journeys, one coast. One line explains how the kitchen works. The menu changes completely four times a year, and partly every time the market brings in something new.

There are two menus, side by side, each on its own card with the price set large in the corner, the way a printed menu would show it.

Aromas de la Costa, at 35 euros, is the shorter route: the aromas of the sea and tropical fruit, the essence of IME in a shorter journey. It lists fish from the market and produce from the Costa Tropical, bread from a nearby bakery, and options for coeliacs.

Senda, at 80 euros, is the long menu: the full IME experience, course by course, from the shore to the vegetable garden. It covers the whole seasonal route, a pairing with Granada wines, and the same care for coeliac guests. In the light theme this card is dark, and in the dark theme it has a gold border, so the eye knows which one is the full experience without being told.

Each card ends with one button: book this menu. A line under both says that prices are per person, drinks are not included, and allergies or intolerances should be mentioned when booking.

Showing prices was a deliberate choice. Some restaurants at this level hide them, and the visitor has to email to find out. That puts off exactly the people who might be planning a birthday or an anniversary and want to know what to expect. Clear prices are a form of hospitality.

The light theme: linen, ink and gold, for the menus, the produce and the booking form.

candlelit by default

Every site in this run so far has had a light theme and a dark theme. This one is the first where dark is the starting point.

A tasting menu is mostly a dinner, and the room is lit low. So the site opens in its dark version: near-black, #0B0A09, warm off-white text, #F2ECE4, and a muted gold, #C49664, for anything you can press. The light theme is linen and ink, #FAF8F4 and #17130F, with a deeper gold, #A0733F. A small sun and moon button in the header switches between them, and the site remembers your choice the next time you visit.

The type is a pairing I have wanted to use for a while: Instrument Serif, a condensed serif with a beautiful italic, for headings, menus and prices, and Manrope, a clean sans, for everything else. The logo is a thin handwritten ime, in gold.

Dark is the default. The moon and sun button switches the theme and remembers the choice.

the cellar and the gift

Two smaller sections follow, and both matter more than their size suggests.

The first is the cellar, bodega. Heading: una carta breve, elegida con intención, a short list, chosen with intention. The text explains that the list comes from years of experience in viticulture: wines with personality, with Granada’s vineyards in the lead, chosen to go with each course. Beside it is a photograph of a glass of red wine standing among the vines. There is no long table of bottles and vintages. A short list is the point, and the button simply says ask about the pairing.

The second is the gift. Regala IME, give IME. The heading is regala una noche para recordar, give a night to remember. Any of the tasting menus can be turned into a gift, for a birthday, an anniversary or simply to say thank you. On the left is a gift card drawn as an object, dark with the gold IME signature and the words un viaje para regalar, a journey to give. The button, buy a gift card, goes straight to the gift page the restaurant already runs. I did not build a new shop. The existing one works, and the job of the concept is to make it easier to find.

Gift cards are a quiet part of the business for many good restaurants. People who have eaten somewhere special want to send their parents, their friends, their best client. A visible, well-presented gift section gives them a reason to.

The produce, the cellar and the gift card, each given its own space.

opening hours, then a table

The last section on the page is called visítanos, visit us, and it puts the hours first. Monday to Wednesday, closed. Thursday to Saturday, lunch from 13:30 to 16:00 and dinner from 20:30 to 23:00. Sunday, lunch only, from 13:30 to 16:00. Sunday in July and August, dinner from 20:30 to 23:00. Under the hours are the address, Calle Francisco Díaz Cardona 2 in Motril, which opens in maps, the phone number and the email address.

Next to the hours is the booking request, reserva tu mesa. First the date and the number of guests. Once a date is chosen, the form offers only the times the kitchen is actually serving that day, in half-hour steps for lunch, dinner or both. Choose a Monday, Tuesday or Wednesday and it says, politely, that the restaurant is closed and suggests Thursday to Sunday. Choose a Sunday in August and it offers dinner instead of lunch. Then the menu: Aromas de la Costa, Senda, or we will decide at the table. Then name, phone, and a field for allergies, celebrations or anything else the kitchen should know.

The button says request a booking, and that is exactly what it does. It prepares an email to the restaurant with everything filled in, ready to send. The restaurant confirms. I did not pretend the concept was a full reservation system. A small restaurant with a handful of tables usually prefers to see every request and answer it personally, and the page respects that.

The hours come first. The form only offers times when the kitchen is open on the chosen day.

on a phone

Most people will look at this site on a phone, often on the same day they want to book. On a small screen everything stacks in the same order: the story, the produce, the menus, the cellar, the gift, the hours.

Two buttons stay pinned to the bottom of the screen the whole time: call, and book a table. They are within reach of a thumb wherever you are on the page. Someone who has already decided does not need to scroll to the end to find the form.

The menu opens over the whole screen with a circular reveal that starts from the menu button in the corner, like a curtain drawn from one side. Inside are the five sections, set large in the serif: experience, menus, cellar, give IME, visit us. Below them are the book a table button, the opening hours in one short line, the phone number and Instagram. Everything a guest needs to make up their mind fits on that one screen.

The menus on a phone, in both themes, with call and book always within reach.

The full-screen menu opens with a circular reveal: sections, booking, hours and contact.

spanish first, english one tap away

IME’s own website is in Spanish, and so is the concept, first. But the Costa Tropical also gets visitors from abroad, and plenty of people living on this coast read English more comfortably than Spanish.

So there is an EN button in the header. Press it, and every piece of text on the page changes to English: the headings, the menus, the opening hours, the form labels, the buttons. It is not a machine translation added on top. Every line has its English version written alongside the Spanish, so both read properly.

why I think this one deserves a look

Every day in this run has its own job. A builder needed a first clear page. A theatre needed an order. A family restaurant needed to show many reasons to walk in. A property practice needed to put a person at the front.

Espacio IME needed something closer to the kitchen itself: restraint, good materials and attention to small things. A gold line beside a quotation. A plate rising at the foot of the opening screen. Prices set like a printed menu. A booking form that knows the kitchen is closed on Tuesdays.

I will say it plainly: I think this one deserves a look from Awwwards. If it gets one, good. If it does not, the page still does what it was made for, which is to sit next to a Michelin listing without looking out of place.

One button in the header, remembered on your next visit.

an independent concept

Espacio IME did not hire me, and this is not their website. The chef’s story, the menus and prices, the produce, the hours, the address and the guide listings come from what the restaurant and the guides already publish. I have not changed any facts. What I changed is the order, the type, the tone and how the page behaves on a phone.

I have no figures on bookings or visits, and I will not make any up. If nobody at IME wants this, the concept stays where it is as day five. If they do, the rest is practical: their words where I have filled in, new photographs for each season’s menu, the booking requests sent wherever they want them, and the site moved onto espacioime.es.

if your kitchen is better than your website

You may not run a tasting-menu restaurant. Many small businesses on this coast are in the same position, though: what they make is better than how they appear online. A bakery that wins awards and has a two-line website. A winery with a beautiful cellar and a page that is mostly a phone number. A hotel with ten perfect rooms and a booking widget from 2015.

What helps is the same as here. Put the people and the produce first. Show the prices if you can. Give the guest one calm way to ask for what they want. Let the design be as careful as the work.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If that sounds like your business, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The concept is here, and Espacio IME’s own site is here, so you can compare the two. Five down, ninety-five to go.

entry.title: the website that looks after itself
entry.summary: Why the brochure website is fading, what it means when people say a site can now look after itself, and what is worth paying for, explained without the jargon.
entry.content:
A question I hear from almost every client, usually near the end of the first call: “Once the website is finished, that’s it, right? I don’t have to keep paying for it?”

It is a fair question. For twenty years the answer was more or less yes. You paid someone to build the site, they handed it over, and it sat there like a printed brochure. Sometimes it was updated. More often it was forgotten.

This week I read a piece on DataDrivenInvestor called The Slow Death of the Static Website. Its argument, in short, is that the small business website is changing from a brochure that needs constant hands-on care into something closer to a system that can keep itself up to date, because it is now connected to the other tools the business already uses. It is written for people who build websites, and it is full of words like APIs, content management systems and autonomous agents.

This note is the version I would give a client across a table. No code, no acronyms without an explanation, and an honest line between what works today, what is still mostly a sales pitch, and what you should still do yourself.

the brochure in the drawer

Think about the last printed brochure your business made. On the day it came back from the printer it was perfect. The prices were right, the photos were new, the opening hours were correct.

Six months later, one price had gone up. A year later, the team photo showed someone who had left. Two years later, the box of brochures was in a drawer and nobody gave them out any more, because they were wrong in three small ways and everybody knew it.

Most small business websites have the same life. The difference is that nobody puts a website in a drawer. It stays online, in public, answering questions for you at three in the morning, with the wrong answers.

A website built this way is what people in my trade call static. The word is technical, and I will come back to it, because it causes some confusion. For now, think of static in the everyday sense: it stays the way it was on the day it was finished, until a person sits down and changes it.

how a website goes quietly out of date

Nobody decides to let their website go stale. It happens one small thing at a time, and usually the customers notice before the owner does.

In the first few months, the opening hours change for summer and nobody updates the site. Someone turns up at a closed door. Then the prices on the menu or the services page drift away from the prices at the till. Then you move to a new booking system, and the old “book now” button still points at the old one. Then a photo goes missing, or a link to a partner breaks because they changed their own site.

Underneath, other things happen that you cannot see. The pieces of software the site depends on need updates, and when they do not get them the site becomes easier to break into. Extra add-ons pile up: a chat bubble, a cookie banner, three tracking tools from three different marketing people. Each one makes the page a little slower on a phone, and slow pages lose visitors and lose ground on Google. The original article calls this silent technical rot, and the name fits. Nothing is broken on any single day. It just gets a little worse each month.

Search is part of it too. Google’s sense of what a good page looks like keeps moving. A site that did well in its first year can slide down without anyone touching it, simply because other sites kept improving and this one did not. Looking after search used to be treated as a list you went through before launch. In practice it never stops.

The awkward part is that the owner almost never sees the website the way a customer does. You know the right opening hours, so your eye slides past the wrong ones on the page. A customer only has the page. For them, whatever it says is the truth about your business, right up until they are standing at a locked door or arguing about a price at the counter. By then the website has cost you something, and nobody can point to the day it happened.

None of this is anyone’s fault. Owners of small businesses are busy running the business. The website is the one employee who never asks for anything, so it is the one who gets forgotten.

How a website goes out of date: never in one go, always a little at a time.

what an API is, without the jargon

The whole article rests on one word that most business owners never need to learn, so here is the short version.

An API is a way for two pieces of software to talk to each other without a person copying things between them. The easiest picture is a waiter. The kitchen does not come out to your table, and you do not walk into the kitchen. The waiter takes a clear request one way and brings a clear answer back the other way.

You already use services that have one of these waiters, even if you have never seen it. Your booking calendar has one. Your Google Business Profile, the box that appears on Google Maps with your hours and reviews, has one. Online shops, stock lists, review sites, newsletter tools and payment providers have them. The weather has one.

When a website is connected to those services, it stops being a copy of your information and starts reading from the source. Change your hours in one place, and the website shows the new hours. Take the last table on Saturday in your booking system, and the website stops offering it. Sell the last flat in a building, and it comes off the list.

That is the first and most useful half of the change the article describes. It needs no artificial intelligence at all. It is mostly careful plumbing.

The website reads from the places where your information already lives, instead of keeping its own copy.

one place to change things

The goal I aim for with clients is simple to say: every piece of information should be typed in one place only.

On day three of my hundred-day challenge I made a homepage concept for Los Arcos, a family bar and restaurant here in Estepona. A restaurant like that keeps three different sets of hours: the restaurant, the bar and the morning café. On the page they sit in tabs, and the large line on the left answers the only question most people have, which is whether the place is open now. A small green mark in the navigation says café open when the café is open.

To be honest about where that concept stands: the hours there are written into the page once, and the page works out the rest from the clock. The next step, if Los Arcos wanted it, would be to read those hours from the same place they already keep them for Google, so a change for Christmas happens once and shows up everywhere. That is the kind of connection I mean. It is not glamorous, and it saves real people a wasted trip.

From the Los Arcos concept: three sets of hours, and one plain answer to “are you open now?”

There is a smaller example on this very site. The homepage of wellyington.github.io now shows the latest entries from this journal, in each of its four languages. Nobody updates that section by hand. When I publish an article, the homepage rebuilds itself a minute later and the new entry is at the top. It is a tiny thing, but it is exactly the idea: write once, and let the rest follow.

The homepage of this site lists the newest journal entries by itself. Publish once, and it appears there too.

from connected to “autonomous”

The second half of the article goes further, and this is where the big words come in. The idea is that a piece of software, usually built on the same kind of artificial intelligence as the chat tools many people now use, sits on top of all those connections and acts on them. Not just reading your hours, but noticing problems and fixing them, writing new pages, and publishing them.

The article lists the kinds of things such a system is connected to: the part of the website where the text is edited, Google Search Console, the visitor statistics, the booking or stock system, and a store of everything the business knows about itself, its tone, its products, its rules.

Google Search Console needs one sentence of explanation, because it comes up in every conversation about this. It is a free report from Google that tells you which searches your website appears for, which pages Google can and cannot read, and what is going wrong. Think of it as the school report your website gets from Google. Most small businesses have never opened theirs, and many have never set it up.

A system with access to that report, your visitor numbers and your bookings can, in principle, see that a page stopped appearing in searches last week, work out why, and suggest a fix before you would ever have noticed. That is the promise. Some of it is real today. Some of it is still a demo.

what this can already do well

Here is what I would trust software to do on a small business website today, with very little risk.

Check, every week, that every link on the site still goes somewhere, and tell you in plain words when one breaks. Measure how fast the main pages load on a phone, and warn you when a new add-on has made them slow. Watch the Search Console report and send you a short summary once a month, written for a person, not for a developer: which searches brought people in, which pages are slipping, what is worth fixing.

Keep lists in step with their source: events from a calendar, rooms or tables from a booking system, properties from a listings file, opening hours from your Google profile. Prepare a first draft of a news post or an event page from your own notes, for you to read and correct. Produce the first version of a translation, so your Spanish, English or Russian visitors are not left out, again for a person to check. Suggest better titles and descriptions for pages that people find in search but rarely click.

None of these jobs is clever. All of them are the kind of job that falls off a busy person’s list and quietly costs money when it does.

what it should not do on its own

The same piece of software that can fix a broken link can also publish a wrong price to everyone who visits, in seconds, with complete confidence. That is the part of the story the enthusiastic articles tend to skip.

There is a good account of this from the people who build these systems. A design magazine recently published a piece by the makers of an autonomous website platform. They set out to make websites run entirely on their own, assuming that was what owners wanted. When real owners used it, the owners hesitated. Almost nobody, it turned out, wants a website that changes itself completely without asking.

That matches what I see. A business owner is happy to let software fix a broken link at night. They are not happy to wake up and find a new paragraph about their prices, their guarantees or their opening on a bank holiday that they never wrote. And they are right. Some things on a website are promises, and promises should come from a person.

So my rule is simple. Software can notice, measure and prepare. A person approves anything that changes what the business says: prices, offers, promises, opening on special days, anything about health, money or the law, anything about another person, and anything in the business’s own voice. The approval can be one tap on a phone. It still matters that it is there.

Software notices and prepares. You approve. Then it publishes and checks whether the change helped.

static is not the enemy

Now the word I promised to come back to. In my trade, static has a technical meaning as well as the everyday one. A technically static website is one where each page is prepared in advance and handed to the visitor as a finished file, rather than being assembled from a database every time someone opens it.

That kind of static is not dying. It is fast, cheap to host, hard to break into and kind to phones on a weak signal. This journal is built that way. So are the hundred-day concepts. Being static in that sense and being out of date are two different things.

The website that is dying is the abandoned brochure: built once, never looked at again, slowly drifting away from the truth. You can avoid that with fast, simple pages that are connected to the places your information lives, rebuilt whenever something changes, and checked regularly by something or someone. The technology behind the curtain matters much less than whether anybody, or anything, is paying attention.

what this means for the money

Here is the honest answer to the question at the start.

The old model was a large fee to build, and then nothing. Or a monthly fee that paid for hosting and very little else. Neither one paid for what actually keeps a website useful, which is somebody noticing when it has drifted.

What makes sense now is usually a smaller build, because simple fast pages do not need to cost a fortune, followed by a modest monthly amount that pays for real work you can see. The checks run every week. The connections to your booking system, your Google profile and your lists are kept working. You get a short report in plain words. And there is a person to call when you need a change that should not be left to a machine.

When someone offers you a monthly plan, ask them what happens in a normal month. If the answer is “we keep it online,” you are paying for a brochure in a drawer. If the answer is a list of things that are checked, updated and reported to you, you are paying for a website that is looked after.

One more thing about money: make sure you own what you pay for. The web address, the text, the photos and the list of your customers’ enquiries should be yours, and you should be able to take them with you if you leave. A website that looks after itself is only good news if it is still yours.

questions to ask before you pay anyone

If you are about to commission a website, or you are unhappy with the one you have, these questions will tell you most of what you need to know. You do not need to understand the technical answers. You only need to hear whether they are clear.

Who owns the web address, and is it in my name? When I change my opening hours or my prices, where do I change them, and how many places is that? Is the site connected to the booking system, the shop or the calendar I already use, or does it keep its own copy? What does the site do on its own, and what does it ask me before it changes? Will I get a regular report I can understand, and how often? How fast is it on a phone with a weak signal? Does it work properly in the languages my customers speak? And if I stop working with you, what do I take with me?

A good answer to the approval question is worth more than anything else on that list.

Eight questions. You don’t need to follow the technical answers, only to hear whether they are clear.

how I build for this

For the businesses I work with along this coast, the practical version looks like this.

The pages are fast and simple, prepared in advance, so they load quickly on a phone at a bus stop. The information that changes, such as hours, events, menus, listings and prices, comes from one place, ideally a place the business already uses. Every change to that information rebuilds the site within minutes. Small checks run every week and report to me, and the important ones also report to the owner. Anything that changes what the business promises is shown to a person before it goes live.

None of that needs the word autonomous. It is closer to a well-run shop: the shelves are restocked from the stockroom, someone walks the floor each morning, and the owner signs off on the prices.

so, is the static website dying?

The brochure website, the one nobody looks after, is fading, and I will not miss it. It sends customers to closed doors and quotes last year’s prices, and it does that while looking perfectly fine to the owner, who rarely visits it.

What replaces it does not have to be a mysterious system that runs your business for you. For most small businesses it is something more modest and more useful: a fast website that reads from the same places you already keep your information, tells you when something is wrong, prepares the dull work, and waits for your yes before it says anything new in your name.

The software has become good at the waiting and the noticing. The saying yes is still your job, and I think it should stay that way.

I am a web designer in Estepona, on the Costa del Sol, and I build websites like this one for businesses across Spain. If you would like to know what your current site would need to stop going out of date, write to me from the main site. Tell me what you do and where, and I will reply in plain language. The article that started this note is The Slow Death of the Static Website on DataDrivenInvestor, if you want the technical version.

entry.title: judgement over volume
entry.summary: Day four of a hundred: a website concept for Nina Estate in Málaga that reads less like a property portal and more like a private practice, with the director, the method and four residences up front.
entry.content:
On 20 November I posted the fourth note of this run, the challenge Ramiah Trask set: a hundred days, a hundred businesses, a hundred websites. Day one was a family builder in the Marina Alta who needed a first clear page. That page is here. Day two was a theatre in Málaga with a full season and no order to it. That one is here. Day three was a family restaurant in my own town, with many reasons to walk in. That one is here. Today the business sells something people take months to decide on.

Nina Estate is a real estate agency in Málaga, with an office on Avenida de Cánovas del Castillo. It works across the city and the Costa del Sol: homes, whole buildings, investments and long-term rentals. It already has a website, at ninaestate.com, which sets out its experience, its properties and its services. My concept is here: Nina Estate, day four.

This is an independent redesign. It is not a collaboration with Nina Estate, nobody there asked for it, and nothing on the page means they approve of it. It lives on my own address for now, like the three before it.

a different kind of agency page

Most property websites are built like shop windows. A search bar at the top, a grid of listings, a price on every card, a phone number in the corner. That works for an agency that wins on volume, with hundreds of homes and a buyer who wants to scroll.

Nina Estate is a different shape of business. A small number of properties, several of them whole buildings. Prices on request. One person, the director, who deals with every client herself. Somebody buying or selling at that level of the luxury market is not mainly choosing a listing. They are choosing who they trust to choose for them.

So I took a different approach from the existing site. Less like a traditional agency, more like a private practice, where the way things are presented, the personal service and the attention to detail are part of what the client gets. The existing site leads with experience, properties and services. The concept leads with the relationship: who you will deal with, how the search will go, and what happens from the first call to the keys.

The idea is simple to say. The website should feel closer to the service it sells.

residences of quiet distinction
